title: Jeremiah 22:20–30
context: The LORD addresses a figure commonly understood as Jerusalem or the royal house, calling her to go up to Lebanon, Bashan, and Abarim and cry out because her lovers, likely her allies, are destroyed. The LORD says he spoke to her in prosperity but she refused to listen, as she had from her youth; her shepherds and lovers will go into captivity, and she who nests in the cedars will be in pain like a woman in labor. The LORD then speaks of Coniah son of Jehoiakim, commonly identified with Jehoiachin (also called Jeconiah, as in 24:1 and 29:2): even if he were the signet ring on the LORD’s right hand, the LORD would pull him off and give him to Nebuchadnezzar, casting him and his mother into a foreign land where he will die (compare 2 Kings 24:8–15). A voice, commonly taken as Jeremiah’s, laments whether Coniah is a despised, broken vessel, and calls on the earth to hear the LORD’s word: record this man as childless, for none of his offspring will prosper sitting on David’s throne. Interpreters discuss how this word relates to 2 Kings 25:27–30 and Jeremiah 52:31–34, where Jehoiachin is released and honored in Babylon, to 1 Chronicles 3:17, which lists sons of Jeconiah, and to the genealogy in Matthew 1:11–12, which includes Jechoniah. Many take childless to mean without a son who reigns, but readers differ on how these texts fit together, and claims about the royal line are best held with care. Haggai 2:23, where the LORD promises to make Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel like a signet, is commonly read as a later echo of 22:24. Arminian and Reformed readers generally read the passage soberly and treat God’s faithfulness to the house of David as shared ground.

verses.text: “Go up to Lebanon, and cry out. Lift up your voice in Bashan, and cry from Abarim; for all your lovers have been destroyed.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the LORD calling a figure, commonly understood as Jerusalem, to cry out from Lebanon, Bashan, and Abarim because her lovers are destroyed. Her allies have failed.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the futility of trusting foreign alliances. Both traditions commonly read the verse as part of the LORD’s sober address to the city in its crisis.

verses.text: I spoke to you in your prosperity, but you said, ‘I will not listen.’ This has been your way from your youth, that you didn’t obey my voice.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the LORD saying he spoke in her prosperity but she refused to listen, as she had from her youth. Refusal became a pattern.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see a long history of disobedience (compare Jeremiah 3:25). Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as an honest account of persistent refusal to hear God.

verses.text: The wind will feed all your shepherds, and your lovers will go into captivity. Surely then you will be ashamed and confounded for all your wickedness.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the wind carrying off her shepherds and her lovers going into captivity. Then she will be ashamed of her wickedness.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see leaders and allies alike swept away in judgment. Both traditions commonly read the verse as showing the emptiness of the city’s false supports.

verses.text: Inhabitant of Lebanon, who makes your nest in the cedars, how greatly to be pitied you will be when pangs come on you, the pain as of a woman in travail!
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the inhabitant of Lebanon, nesting in the cedars, facing pain like a woman in labor. Security among the cedars will not prevent suffering.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the image of cedar palaces as a likely reference to Jerusalem’s royal buildings. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as a sober picture of coming distress.

verses.text: “As I live,” says the LORD, “though Coniah the son of Jehoiakim king of Judah were the signet on my right hand, I would still pluck you from there.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the LORD saying that even if Coniah were the signet on his right hand, he would pull him off. Royal status offers no protection from judgment.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the signet as an image of authority and close association. Both traditions commonly note Haggai 2:23 as a later echo, where the LORD promises to make Zerubbabel like a signet.

verses.text: I would give you into the hand of those who seek your life, and into the hand of them of whom you are afraid, even into the hand of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, and into the hand of the Chaldeans.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the LORD saying he will give Coniah into the hands of those who seek his life, including Nebuchadnezzar and the Chaldeans. His fears will come true.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the word fulfilled in Jehoiachin’s surrender and exile (compare 2 Kings 24:12). Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse within that history.

verses.text: I will cast you out with your mother who bore you into another country, where you were not born; and there you will die.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the LORD saying he will cast Coniah and his mother into a foreign land where he will die. The royal family goes into exile.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the queen mother’s exile also reported in 2 Kings 24:15 and Jeremiah 29:2. Both traditions commonly read the verse as a sober statement of the king’s fate.

verses.text: But to the land to which their soul longs to return, there they will not return.”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see that they will not return to the land their souls long for. Exile brings deep and lasting longing for home.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the grief of permanent exile for the king. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse with sympathy for the human sorrow of being cut off from one’s land.

verses.text: Is this man Coniah a despised broken vessel? Is he a vessel in which no one delights? Why are they cast out, he and his offspring, and cast into a land which they don’t know?
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see a voice, commonly taken as Jeremiah’s, asking whether Coniah is a despised, broken vessel in which no one delights. The lament is tinged with pity.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see sorrow over the king’s rejection and exile with his offspring. Both traditions commonly read the verse as a lament that feels the weight of judgment.

verses.text: O earth, earth, earth, hear the LORD’s word!
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the threefold call to the earth to hear the LORD’s word. The message is solemn and weighty for all who hear.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the repetition as emphasizing the seriousness of what follows. Readers in both traditions commonly read the verse as a solemn introduction to the final word on Coniah.

verses.text: The LORD says, “Record this man as childless, a man who will not prosper in his days; for no more will a man of his offspring prosper, sitting on David’s throne and ruling in Judah.”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the LORD saying to record Coniah as childless, since none of his offspring will prosper on David’s throne. Many take this to mean no son of his will reign.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the word alongside 1 Chronicles 3:17 and Matthew 1:12, which interpreters discuss in different ways. Both traditions commonly hold God’s faithfulness to David as shared ground while holding the details with care.
